analysis.one_liner: Bans drugmakers from delaying cheaper generics by switching patients to reformulated versions.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the bill in April 2025 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but no floor vote has been scheduled since.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug is about to face generic competition, its maker sometimes pulls the original drug off the market and steers patients to a slightly altered version with a later-expiring patent, restarting years without cheaper copies. This tactic is called product hopping. The bill makes product hopping an unfair method of competition under federal antitrust law and lets the Federal Trade Commission sue to stop it and claw back profits. It has cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee with bipartisan support and is waiting for a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and health plans who pay for brand-name drugs. Product hopping can delay generic competition by years; generics typically sell at a fraction of the brand-name price, so blocking the tactic speeds up price drops. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers also benefit because it becomes harder for brand companies to freeze them out of the market.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits product hopping: a brand manufacturer may not withdraw the original drug from the market and sell a reformulated follow-on product with a later-expiring patent in order to block generic or biosimilar competition.

Lets the FTC enforce the ban through administrative proceedings or federal court suits, including stopping the conduct and ordering companies to disgorge unjust profits or pay restitution to those harmed.

Creates a presumption that a hard switch (withdrawing the original drug and selling a follow-on) is anticompetitive once the brand maker has notice that a generic application is pending, with the burden shifting to the company to justify the change.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which could lose monopoly revenue they currently extend through patent games, and potentially face FTC suits and disgorgement of profits.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not directly lower any drug price; it removes one specific tactic. Manufacturers can still use other patent strategies, and generic entry depends on many factors outside this bill.

Drugmakers legitimately improve products for safety or quality reasons. The bill tries to separate the two — it excludes changes the FDA requires and lets manufacturers justify conduct with safety or pro-competitive reasons — but drawing that line in practice will be contentious and litigated, and companies may grow cautious about genuinely beneficial reformulations.

Enforcement depends entirely on the FTC choosing to bring cases, and remedies are equitable (injunctions, disgorgement, restitution), with no automatic penalties, so deterrence depends on agency priorities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — faster generic competition and lower drug prices — is real, since generic versions typically sell for far less than brand prices. The main costs are the risk of chilling legitimate product improvements and the practical difficulty of separating innovation from gaming. The bill's exclusions for FDA-required changes and its justification defenses are an attempt to manage that, though the line will be tested in litigation.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it in April 2025 and it is sitting on the Senate calendar waiting for a floor vote that has not been scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 13, 2025 by Senator Cornyn with Senators Blumenthal, Grassley, and Durbin, giving it sponsorship from both parties.

The Senate Judiciary Committee ordered it reported favorably with an amendment on April 3, 2025, and it was reported and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 43) on April 10, 2025.
No floor vote or further action has occurred since it was placed on the calendar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drugmakers, which so far face no new restrictions and can continue the practices the bill would ban while it waits.

for.name: John Cornyn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban product hopping.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator (IA), reported the bill out of the Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Shepherded the bill through committee and reported it with an amendment in April 2025.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican and cosponsored at introduction by two Democrats and one Republican, and cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee with bipartisan support in April 2025.

industries.note: Product hopping is a way to extend years of patent-protected revenue by switching patients to reformulated versions just before generics arrive. The bill would let the FTC stop that practice and claw back profits, directly reducing a source of extended monopoly revenue.
The bill makes it harder for brand companies to withdraw original drugs or disadvantage them so generics cannot compete, clearing the path for earlier generic and biosimilar entry.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: Earlier generic entry lowers the prices payers and plans negotiate, reducing prescription drug costs across the system.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has bipartisan sponsorship and cleared the Judiciary Committee, but the Senate has taken no floor action in months. Bills sitting on the General Orders calendar frequently stall unless leadership schedules time, and the bill would still need separate action in the House. Its prospects this Congress depend entirely on whether Senate leadership brings it to the floor.
